group.passage: Vincent van Gogh’s “The Starry Night” is one of the most famous paintings in the world. In the two texts below, an art historian describes how the picture came to be, and a physicist explains what scientists have discovered in its swirling sky.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: A Night Seen and Felt
passage_parts.text: Van Gogh painted “The Starry Night” in June 1889, during the year he spent as a patient at a hospital in Saint-Rémy, in the south of France. From his room he could see the hills and fields beyond the walls under a changing sky. The finished work, however, owes as much to his imagination as to his eyes. A quiet village sits beneath the hills, and a dark cypress tree rises in the foreground like a flame. What makes the painting unforgettable is its sky. The stars burn inside rings of light, and great waves of blue and white roll across the night as though the air itself were alive. Van Gogh was not trying to copy exactly what the night looked like; he wanted to show what it felt like. Today the painting hangs in the Museum of Modern Art in New York, where it draws visitors from all over the world.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Order in the Swirls
passage_parts.text: My work as a physicist is on turbulent flow, the irregular motion of air and water that you can see in rising smoke or a fast river. Few paintings convey that restless motion as vividly as “The Starry Night.” In the 1940s, the Russian mathematician Andrei Kolmogorov showed that such flow hides a kind of order: large eddies break into smaller ones in a predictable way, passing their energy down the chain. In 2006, researchers in Mexico looked at how brightness changes across the painting and found the same mathematical pattern. Research published in 2024 went further, finding that the sizes of its fourteen main swirls also fit Kolmogorov’s description, even though van Gogh died more than a decade before Kolmogorov was born. Still, these results should be taken with a grain of salt. A painting does not move, so it cannot literally contain turbulent flow, and no one is suggesting that van Gogh knew the mathematics. The likelier explanation is that he was an unusually patient observer of nature, who caught with a brush what science would only later put into equations.

translation_zh.text:
文森．梵谷的〈星夜〉是世界上最有名的畫作之一。在下面兩篇短文中，一位藝術史學者描述這幅畫是怎麼來的，一位物理學者則說明科學家在它旋轉的天空中發現了什麼。

A　看見的夜，感受到的夜
梵谷在 1889 年 6 月畫下〈星夜〉，那一年他以病人的身分住在法國南部聖雷米的一家醫院。從房間裡，他看得到圍牆外的山丘和田野，以及頭頂變幻的天空。然而，完成的畫作靠想像的部分和靠眼睛的部分一樣多。一座寧靜的村莊座落在山丘下，一棵深色的柏樹像火焰般在前景升起。讓這幅畫令人難忘的，是它的天空。星星在一圈圈光環中燃燒，藍白相間的巨浪在夜空中翻滾，彷彿空氣本身是活的。梵谷並不是想照實描繪夜晚的樣子，他想畫出的是夜晚給人的感受。如今這幅畫掛在紐約的現代藝術博物館，吸引來自世界各地的參觀者。

B　漩渦中的秩序
身為物理學者，我研究的是亂流——在上升的煙霧或湍急的河水中看得到的、空氣和水的不規則運動。很少有畫作能像〈星夜〉一樣，把那種躁動不安的流動表現得如此生動。1940 年代，俄國數學家安德烈．柯爾莫哥洛夫證明這種流動隱藏著某種秩序：大的渦流以可預測的方式分裂成小的渦流，把能量一路往下傳。2006 年，墨西哥的研究人員分析了這幅畫中亮度的變化，發現了同樣的數學模式。2024 年發表的研究更進一步，發現畫中十四個主要漩渦的大小也符合柯爾莫哥洛夫的描述——儘管梵谷過世十多年後，柯爾莫哥洛夫才出生。不過，這些結果應該有保留地看待。畫作不會動，所以不可能真的包含亂流，也沒有人認為梵谷懂得其中的數學。比較可能的解釋是，他是一位格外有耐心的大自然觀察者，用畫筆捕捉到了科學後來才寫成方程式的東西。
